title: Audio Capture
summary: Audio capture is the recording of sound through a host microphone or through a voice and video calling application that already holds the device. Malware reaches the hardware either by calling the operating system media interfaces or by attaching to a conferencing process, and the second route is quieter because no new device access event is generated. Recordings are normally written to disk as media files and exfiltrated later, so the artefacts are temporary files, unexpected audio file creation, and a process holding the microphone while no call is in progress. Modern operating systems show an indicator when the microphone is active, and per application privacy permissions decide which binaries may use it at all. Telling malicious capture apart from legitimate conferencing comes down to which process holds the device, under which user account, and at what time of day, rather than to the recording itself.

beginner.definition: Audio capture means recording sound with a computer microphone. An attacker can use malware or a calling application to record conversations. The recordings are saved as files and sent out of the network later.
beginner.whyItMatters: People say things out loud that they would never write down. Examples are a password given over the phone or the details of a deal. A microphone turns a normal office into a listening device. Laptops usually have a microphone built in, so no extra hardware is needed. Recordings also take time to find, because audio files look like ordinary media.
howItWorks: Malware or a script calls the operating system interface that gives access to the microphone.
Some samples instead attach to a voice or video call application that already holds the device.
Audio is recorded in short chunks or as one long file, depending on the tool.
The recording is written to a temporary or hidden file on disk.
The file is packed and sent to the attacker later, often together with other collected data.
Some tools start recording only when sound is detected, which saves space and creates fewer files.
beginner.example: Imagine a meeting room where someone leaves a phone on the table with a recording application running. The room looks normal and the door stays locked. Everyone speaks freely because they cannot see that the phone is listening. Later the recording is sent away, and nobody in the building ever hears it.
takeaways: A microphone can be used without new hardware and without any obvious change.
Check which process holds the microphone when no call is running.
Microphone permissions and in use indicators are your fastest checks.

objectives: Explain how malware records sound through operating system media interfaces.
Describe how an attacker can record through a conferencing application instead of the device.
Identify the file and process artefacts that audio capture leaves behind.
Explain how microphone permissions and in use indicators help a defender.
Describe why audio capture is difficult to notice after the recording is finished.
